speakers: Campbell R. Harvey (Duke University; Man Group)
summary: Question: should carry, momentum and value be traded directionally (time series) or cross-asset (long-short)? Method: simple signals on 87 futures/forward/swap markets in 4 asset classes, 1990-2015, gross of costs, CS top/bottom-3 vs TS sign x 1/N. Conclusion: value works best CS, momentum TS, carry both; CS = TS hedged for the global factor, so global-factor trend and signal vs asset correlation decide; combined Sharpe 1.4-1.6.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: We contrast the time-series and cross-sectional performance of three popular investment strategies: carry, momentum and value.
claims.claim: The paper compares directional (time-series) and cross-asset (cross-sectional) implementations of carry, momentum and value to learn which market conditions favour each setting.
claims.testable: yes - both implementations are fully specified later

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: In a cross-asset strategy that is market neutral, the dominant factor is effectively hedged out.
claims.claim: A market-neutral cross-asset portfolio removes the dominant first principal component (the market), so it only harvests predictability in the remaining factors.
claims.exact_rule: Cross-sectional (market-neutral) portfolio = directional portfolio minus exposure to first PC/market factor
claims.testable: yes - PCA of returns and regression of strategy P&L on PC1

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: if the market factor is trending, then it is more likely time-series momentum will be profitable than cross-sectional momentum.
claims.claim: When the common (market) factor itself trends, directional momentum captures it while cross-sectional momentum hedges it away, so time-series momentum should win.
claims.indicator: trend in first principal component / market factor
claims.direction: prefer TS momentum over CS momentum when market factor trends
claims.conditions: works when the global factor is trending
claims.testable: yes - condition CS vs TS momentum spread on PC1 autocorrelation

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: We fill this gap by providing an analysis of both the time- series and cross-section using a broad number of asset classes: equity, fixed income, currencies and commodities.
claims.claim: Prior work studied either TS momentum (Moskowitz et al. 2012) or CS value/momentum (Asness et al. 2013); this paper compares both implementations for four asset classes.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: we are testing three strategies that are select - they are popular because they have worked.
claims.claim: Because the three styles were chosen for having worked (factor proliferation critique of Harvey et al. 2015), their average returns are biased upward and the paper focuses on conditions, not profitability.
claims.testable: no - selection bias cannot be tested inside the sample

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Important drivers are the correlation of asset returns, the correlation of the information that drives markets (some of which is unobservable), as well as the correlation of the trading signals.
claims.claim: The difference between directional and cross-asset performance is said to be driven by asset-return correlation, information correlation and signal correlation; a full treatment is deferred to a future paper.
claims.indicator: average pairwise asset correlation; average pairwise signal correlation
claims.testable: partly - information correlation is unobservable; asset and signal correlations are measurable

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: We define carry as the difference between the spot and the forward price of an asset – in other words the profit on a long forward position if prices do not change.
claims.claim: Carry is the spot-forward gap, i.e. the return of a long forward if the spot price stays unchanged; the simple trade buys the forward when carry is positive and sells it when negative.
claims.exact_rule: carry = (spot - forward)/forward; long forward if carry > 0, short if carry < 0
claims.direction: long positive carry, short negative carry

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: which cannot happen by Jensen’s inequality. This means that forward prices cannot be unbiased predictors of future spot prices.
claims.claim: Because forward unbiasedness cannot hold simultaneously for a price and its reciprocal (Jensen's inequality), forwards cannot be unbiased predictors of future spot, so uncovered interest parity cannot hold exactly.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: By standard arbitrage, the forward price is equal to the spot price compounded at the risk-free rate minus the dividend yield:
claims.claim: By cost-of-carry arbitrage F = S*exp((r-d)(T-t)), so carry is positive when the dividend yield exceeds the risk-free rate (forward below spot).
claims.exact_rule: F_t,T = S_t * exp((r - d)(T - t))

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: For practical purposes, readers can think of forwards and futures as equivalent in this section.
claims.claim: Footnote 1: forwards and futures are treated as equivalent in the theory section (ignores marking-to-market differences).

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: There is a systematic forward bias. Forward prices are lower than expected spot prices for positive beta assets, that is most assets.
claims.claim: Under CAPM, E(S_T)/F = exp(beta*pi*(T-t)) > 1, so long forward positions in positive-beta assets earn a positive expected P&L regardless of carry.
claims.exact_rule: E_t(S_T)/F_t,T = exp(beta*pi*(T-t)); expected P&L = S_t e^{(r-d)(T-t)}[e^{beta pi (T-t)} - 1]
claims.testable: partly - needs beta and equity premium estimates

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: The sign of the forward bias is independent of carry: the ratio of expected spot to forward depends on βπ, not on r − d.
claims.claim: In the plain CAPM the carry level (r-d) does not predict the forward bias, so carry trades need a richer pricing model to be profitable.
claims.testable: partly - regress forward bias on carry

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: With the dividend factor - a proxy for the value factor as we shall see below - the forward bias is now correlated with carry.
claims.claim: Adding a dividend (value) factor with loading gamma makes E(S)/F = exp((beta*pi + gamma*(d - dbar))(T-t)), so higher dividend yield means higher carry and a more profitable carry trade; carry and value are linked.
claims.exact_rule: E_t(S_T)/F = exp((beta*pi + gamma*(d - d_mkt))(T-t)); higher d -> higher carry -> larger forward bias
claims.indicator: dividend yield relative to market dividend yield
claims.testable: yes - cross-sectional regression of forward bias on dividend yield

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: high-yielding currencies tend to depreciate whereas low-yielding currencies hold their own in low domestic consumption states.
claims.claim: Lustig and Verdelhan (2007): low-yield currencies hedge bad consumption states, so they earn lower expected returns than high-yielders, a risk-based explanation of FX carry.
claims.conditions: carry loses in low consumption states

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Breeden (1986) derives equilibrium relationships between interest rates, growth and other parameters from optimal consumption and production models
claims.claim: Breeden (1986) is cited for equilibrium links between interest rates and growth, used later to define rates value.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: find the strategy is rela- tively uncorrelated with factors such as value and momentum but is partially explained by recession and volatility risk.
claims.claim: Koijen et al. (2013): carry across asset classes is largely uncorrelated with value and momentum and partly compensates recession and volatility risk.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: This trade can be profitable because high-yields are associated with non-diversifiable risk factors such as political turmoil or wavering property rights or persistently high inflation.
claims.claim: FX carry (long high-yield, short low-yield) pays because high yields compensate non-diversifiable risks such as political turmoil, weak property rights and persistent inflation, and can reflect unrealised jump (peso) risk.
claims.testable: partly - peso risk may not show in sample

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: a high yield on a currency can reflect a central bank just about to gain or regain anti-inflation credentials that will make its currency more desirable.
claims.claim: An alternative FX carry story: a high yield may signal a central bank about to gain credibility, after which the currency appreciates.
claims.testable: partly - needs measure of credibility gains

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: speculators are incented by hedgers to sell contangoed futures and buy backwardated futures.
claims.claim: Hedging pressure goes both ways (producers short, consumers like airlines long), so speculators are paid to buy backwardated and sell contangoed futures; Keynes' normal backwardation is not the norm today.
claims.testable: yes - sort on curve slope; hedging pressure data (COT)

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: A low level of inventories may result in a high convenience yield, hence a backwardation (Working, 1933; Kaldor, 1939 and Schwartz 1997). Because inventories take time to rebuild, profits from the carry trade can be persistent.
claims.claim: Theory of storage: low inventories raise the convenience yield and cause backwardation; since inventories rebuild slowly, commodity carry profits persist.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Rates tend to roll down the curve: this translates into excess returns for fixed income investors.
claims.claim: Term structures are usually upward sloping (liquidity premium or preferred habitat), and rolling down the curve gives fixed income investors excess returns, the basis of rates carry.
claims.direction: long bonds/receive fixed where curve is steep

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Asset returns appear to exhibit negative autocorrelation over very short periods (less than one month) and longer time periods (more than three years) while the sweet spot for momentum, or positively auto-correlated, strategies is around 6-12 months.
claims.claim: Returns reverse at horizons under one month and over three years but persist at 6-12 months, so momentum signals should use intermediate lookbacks (conventional: buy past-year winners, sell losers).
claims.direction: long past winners, short past losers
claims.conditions: reversal below 1 month and beyond 3 years

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: On the risk end of the spectrum, momentum performs because high-momentum assets are more sensitive to macroeconomic
claims.claim: Risk-based momentum: high-momentum assets load more on macro risk such as industrial production growth (Liu and Zhang 2008).

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: a cross-section of past winners with high realized returns has higher expected returns and ends up outperforming a cross-section of past losers (Conrad and Kaul, 1988).
claims.claim: Conrad and Kaul (1988): if realised and expected returns are correlated, cross-sectional dispersion in expected returns alone generates momentum.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: investors underreact to news either because they display conservatism bias and are slow updating their beliefs (Barberis, Shleifer and Vishny, 1998) or because they do not receive and update information at the same time (Hong and Stein, 1999).
claims.claim: Behavioural momentum: underreaction from conservatism (BSV 1998) or gradual information diffusion (Hong and Stein 1999) makes prices adjust slowly.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: behavioral biases can generate momentum when fund flows exhibit inertia and the market under-reacts to expected future flows.
claims.claim: Vayanos and Woolley (2013): inertial fund flows that the market under-anticipates create persistent returns until large deviations from fundamentals cause a reversal.
claims.conditions: reverses after large deviation from fundamentals

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: At equilibrium, today’s price is positively correlated to yesterday’s price and only partially reflects the fundamental asset value.
claims.claim: Grinblatt and Han (2002) disposition-effect model: with a share of disposition investors, the clearing price is P_t = w F_t + (1-w) P_{t-1}, w = 1/(1+mu*alpha), so prices partially adjust and trend toward fundamentals.
claims.exact_rule: P_t = w F_t + (1 - w) P_{t-1}, w = 1/(1 + mu*alpha)

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Because recent policy moves (negative nominal rates, open-ended quantitative easing, implicit policy focus on wealth effects) are unprecedented and unfamiliar, people rely more on heuristics
claims.claim: The AHL/MSS advisory board judges momentum to be behavioural ('qualified yes'): unprecedented policy pushes investors to heuristics and anchoring, which with liquid markets and fast information diffusion favours persistence of slow momentum.
claims.indicator: policy regime novelty (negative rates, open-ended QE)

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Value can be defined as the difference between a fundamental asset price and its prevailing market price.
claims.claim: Value = fundamental price minus market price; the question is whether a fundamental price exists and what makes prices revert to it.
claims.testable: partly - fundamental price must be modelled

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: With logarithmic utility functions and a log-normally distributed consumption, we can solve for the equilibrium real interest rate
claims.claim: A two-period consumption model with log utility gives the equilibrium real rate r = g + rho - sigma^2/2 (r = g in a deterministic model), the anchor for rates value.
claims.exact_rule: r = g + rho - sigma^2/2; deterministic: r = g

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: When capital is free to move across countries, there is evidently a tendency for real rates of return to converge.
claims.claim: With free capital mobility real rates converge, so a higher domestic real rate attracts excess demand for domestic fixed income; the real-rate differential is another rates value metric.
claims.direction: long bonds of countries with high real rates

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: meaning that the equity yield is the sum of the dividend growth and the dividend yield.
claims.claim: Gordon model: R = g + D/P and ERP = g - r + D/P; if r = g the equity risk premium equals the dividend yield.
claims.exact_rule: ERP = g - r + D/P; with r = g, ERP = D/P

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: the real interest rate at equilibrium is r = γg + ρ − γ 2 σ 2 . Note that CRRA utility functions become logarithmic for
claims.claim: Footnote 2: with CRRA utility the equilibrium real rate is r = gamma*g + rho - gamma^2 sigma^2/2.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Dividend yields can therefore be used as a measure of value for broad equity markets. High dividend yields may indicate that stocks are cheap against bonds
claims.claim: Dividend yield measures broad equity market value; a high yield signals stocks are cheap versus bonds.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Similarly, high price-to-book ratios are a presumption of expensiveness.
claims.claim: Price-to-book (a cousin of Tobin's Q, where Q > 1 means replacing assets is cheaper than buying the firm) is another equity value measure; high P/B means expensive.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: This would all suggest that value investing in commodity space is tantamount to positioning for long mean-reversion cycles.
claims.claim: Commodity prices mean-revert because high prices raise supply (and low prices cut it) and competition pulls prices to production cost, so commodity value bets on long mean-reversion cycles.
claims.indicator: real price vs long-run average / production cost

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: One can see how PPP is more a tautology than a theory - the only issue being how much frictions
claims.claim: PPP is the intuitive FX value anchor; deviations from it reflect frictions (transport costs, tariffs, sticky prices, capital flows, policy), which determine how far real exchange rates stray.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Much like theories of momentum, theories of value can be based on rational or behavioral stories.
claims.claim: The value premium has rational and behavioural explanations, as momentum does.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Dornbusch's overshooting model (1976) is an example of a rational story that explains large deviations from PPP.
claims.claim: Dornbusch (1976): with sticky goods prices and UIP, an unexpected money supply increase lowers domestic rates and makes the currency depreciate instantly beyond its PPP level, creating a rational large deviation from PPP.
claims.direction: currency overshoots down after surprise easing, then appreciates toward PPP

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: when interest rates are lower than growth as is currently the case, dividend yields tend to underestimate the equity risk premium.
claims.claim: Footnote 3: dividend yield is time-varying and not a pure value gauge; with rates below growth it understates the ERP, while leverage may imply a lower ERP.
claims.conditions: r < g biases dividend yield as ERP proxy

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: This mechanism is reminiscent of the euro sudden depreciation in response to the unanticipated loosening of monetary policy in Europe recently.
claims.claim: The recent euro fall after surprise ECB easing illustrates overshooting; such moves create value opportunities in slow-adjusting assets such as euro-denominated real estate, which stayed sticky.
claims.direction: buy slow-adjusting assets priced in the overshooting currency

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: While this model is arbitrage free - the value premium is perfectly neutralized by the carry
claims.claim: In the Dornbusch model the expected value gain is exactly offset by negative carry, so value and carry are linked and FX value alone need not pay.
claims.testable: yes - value and carry return correlation

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Hansen Heaton and Li (1998) attribute the out-performance of value portfolios (relative to growth portfolios) to a higher long term exposure to consumption risk.
claims.claim: Risk-based equity value: value stocks carry more long-run consumption risk (Hansen, Heaton and Li; reference list dates it 2008).

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: value strategies outperform glamour strategies because investors put excessive weight on past history and just equate well-run firms with good investments.
claims.claim: Behavioural value: investors extrapolate past history and confuse good firms with good investments (Lakonishok, Shleifer and Vishny 1994).

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Benartzi and Thaler (1995) explain how investors with prospect-theory type of utility end up buying large amounts of T- bills despite a large equity risk premium.
claims.claim: Benartzi-Thaler myopic loss aversion and Maenhout ambiguity aversion are cited for a large equity risk premium.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: The sample period starts in January 1990 and ends in April 2015.
claims.claim: Data: Bloomberg, Global Financial Data and Man-AHL database, Jan 1990-Apr 2015; 26 equity futures, 14 interest rate swaps, 31 currency pairs, 16 commodity futures, all in USD.
claims.exact_rule: universe: 26 equity index futures, 14 10Y IRS, 31 FX vs USD, 16 commodity futures; sample 1990-01 to 2015-04; USD returns
claims.data_needed: Bloomberg, Global Financial Data, Man-AHL proprietary database

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: We used mid-market prices and do not therefore account for trading costs (which we discuss later).
claims.claim: All results use mid prices and are gross of trading costs (the later discussion only mentions low funding costs, never quantifies trading costs).

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: We used the 3 month FX-forward to imply the carry, as shown below:
claims.claim: FX carry = 4 x (Spot / 3M forward - 1), an annualised forward premium.
claims.exact_rule: Carry_t = 4 * (Spot_t / Fwd3M_t - 1); positive when forward below spot (high-yield currency vs USD)
claims.data_needed: FX spot and 3-month outright forwards vs USD

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: We used the first two futures of each index and computed a raw carry signal as follows:
claims.claim: Equity index raw carry = (F1 - F2)/F2 divided by (T2 - T1), the annualised slope between the first two futures.
claims.exact_rule: Raw_Carry_t = (Fut_T1 - Fut_T2)/Fut_T2 / (T2 - T1)
claims.data_needed: first and second equity index futures prices and expiries

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: For every month m, we compute a seasonality adjustment which is the average difference between the raw carry and its 1Y moving average at time t for all the m-month business days in the sample:
claims.claim: Equity carry is de-seasonalised: for each calendar month m, subtract the average (to date) of raw carry minus its 1-year moving average across all past business days in month m (removes dividend seasonality).
claims.exact_rule: Adj_t = mean over all business days in calendar month m up to t of [Raw_Carry - 1Y_MA(Raw_Carry)]; Carry_t = Raw_Carry_t - Adj_t

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Then, to remove this seasonal effect in the carry computation, we used the first future and the contract exactly expiring one year later.
claims.claim: Commodity carry uses the front future and the contract expiring exactly one year later, to avoid seasonal curve shapes (agriculture, energy); as printed the formula is (F_{T1+1} - F_{T1})/F_{T1+1}.
claims.exact_rule: Carry_t = (Fut_{T1+1y} - Fut_{T1}) / Fut_{T1+1y} (as printed; sign appears to measure contango)

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Carry is meant as ”carry + roll down”. We used the following formula:
claims.claim: Rates carry = (10Y swap - short fixing)/modified duration + (10Y - 7Y swap)/3 (roll-down), with duration = (1 - (1 + S10)^-10)/S10.
claims.exact_rule: Carry_t = (S10Y_t - Fixing_t)/Duration_t + (S10Y_t - S7Y_t)/3; Duration_t = (1 - (1 + S10Y_t)^-10)/S10Y_t
claims.data_needed: 10Y and 7Y swap rates, short-rate fixing (e.g. 3M Libor)
claims.direction: receive fixed where carry+roll is high

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: For all asset classes, we used a CTA-momentum signal, based on the cross over of exponentially weighted moving averages.
claims.claim: Momentum uses one CTA-style EWMA-crossover signal for all asset classes: three short/long pairs S=(8,16,32), L=(24,48,96) where n maps to decay lambda=(n-1)/n and half-life log(0.5)/log(1-1/n).
claims.direction: long when short EWMA > long EWMA

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: We normalize with a moving standard deviation as a measure of the realized 3-months normal volatility (PW=63)
claims.claim: Each crossover x_k = EWMA(S_k) - EWMA(L_k) is divided by the 63-day rolling standard deviation of price, then by its own 252-day rolling standard deviation.
claims.exact_rule: y_k = x_k / RunStDev(P, 63); z_k = y_k / RunStDev(y_k, 252)

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: We calculate an intermediate signal for each k=1,2,3 via a response function R
claims.claim: Each normalised crossover passes through R(z) = z*exp(-z^2/4)/0.89, which peaks near |z| = 1.4 and fades for extreme values; the final signal is the equal-weight (1/3) average over the three speeds.
claims.conditions: response function cuts exposure to very stretched trends

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: We used relative PPP (purchasing power parity) as value indicator:
claims.claim: FX value = log real spot minus its historical mean (relative PPP), with real spot = nominal spot x CPI_ccy1/CPI_ccy2.
claims.exact_rule: Value_t = log(Spot_real_t) - mean(log(Spot_real)); Spot_real = Spot_{CCY1/CCY2} * CPI_CCY1 / CPI_CCY2 (averaging window not stated; sign of trade not stated)
claims.data_needed: FX spot vs USD; CPI for each country and US
claims.indicator: real exchange rate deviation from mean

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: We used dividend yield as value indicator:
claims.claim: Equity index value = dividend yield (raw level, not relative to history or bonds).
claims.exact_rule: Value_t = DivYield_t

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Value is defined as today’s deflated price divided by the deflated historical average price, where history is the expanding window of all prices available:
claims.claim: Commodity value = US-CPI-deflated price divided by its expanding-window historical average.
claims.exact_rule: Adj.Price_t = Price_t / US_CPI_t; Value_t = Adj.Price_t / mean(Adj.Price over all history to t); presumably short high values

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: We defined value, in the rate space, as the difference between the 10Y swap rate and the most recent nominal GDP growth rate (release quarterly):
claims.claim: Rates value = 10Y swap rate minus the latest nominal GDP growth rate, lagged three months (footnote 4); a high spread over growth means cheap bonds.
claims.exact_rule: Value_t = S10Y_t - nominal GDP growth (latest quarterly release, 3-month lag)
claims.data_needed: 10Y swap rates; quarterly nominal GDP growth
claims.direction: receive (long bonds) where rate exceeds growth

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: We used a three month lag for the GDP growth rate.
claims.claim: Footnote 4: GDP growth enters with a three-month lag to approximate publication delay.
claims.exact_rule: GDP growth lagged 3 months

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: We tested both definitions and the results were quite similar.
claims.claim: Using 10Y swap minus year-on-year CPI inflation instead of GDP growth gives similar results; GDP version reported.
claims.exact_rule: alternative: Value_t = S10Y_t - CPI yoy

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: we ranked all the assets according to the magnitude of the signal and took long/short positions on the six most extreme assets (three on each side).
claims.claim: Cross-sectional portfolio: per style and asset class rank assets on the signal, go long the top three and short the bottom three with equal weights (independent of signal size), rebalanced daily.
claims.exact_rule: rank by signal; long top 3, short bottom 3; equal weights; daily rebalance

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: We used the six most extreme assets. Afterwards, we tested for other configurations and the results were compa- rable
claims.claim: Footnote 5: other numbers of extreme assets gave comparable results (no figures shown).

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: we ranked all indices by dividend yield, and took long positions on the three highest dividend paying indices and short positions on the three lowest dividend paying indices.
claims.claim: Example: equity value is long the three highest-yield indices and short the three lowest, held one business day.
claims.exact_rule: daily: long 3 highest DY indices, short 3 lowest DY
claims.direction: long high DY, short low DY

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: we computed the ex-ante volatility of each of the portfolios and scaled their allocations for an annualized volatility of 15% per portfolio.
claims.claim: When combining asset classes each portfolio is scaled to 15% ex-ante annual volatility; styles are combined with equal weights because volatility comes mainly from asset-class choice.
claims.exact_rule: scale each {asset class, style} portfolio to 15% ex-ante vol; combine styles equal-weight

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: within every asset class, we consider the universe of N assets and take positions equivalent to N 1 .
claims.claim: Time-series portfolio: same signals, each of N assets gets a 1/N position, long or short by the signal sign; otherwise identical to the cross-sectional build.
claims.exact_rule: position_i = sign(signal_i) / N within asset class
claims.testable: partly - zero point for always-positive signals (dividend yield, deflated price ratio) not stated

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: {“FX”, “carry”} and {“FX”, “value”} are two exceptions here because mean reversion in FX is slower than in equity and commodities.
claims.claim: FX carry and FX value are not fully rebalanced daily: 1/252 of the book is renewed each day and each tranche is held one year, because FX mean reversion is slow.
claims.exact_rule: each day open a new 1/252 tranche from today's signal, close the tranche opened 1 year ago

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: With one exception, all the Sharpe ratios are positive with an average of 0.40 per asset class.
claims.claim: Cross-sectional single-style Sharpe ratios are positive except rates momentum; all-asset Sharpe is 0.75 value, 1.27 carry, 0.42 momentum, carry being best.
claims.reported_result: Table 1A CS Sharpe 1990-2015 gross: FX V0.42 C0.67 M0.74; EQ V0.39 C0.33 M0.01; Commo V0.07 C0.77 M0.45; IR V0.56 C0.76 M-0.31; All Asset V0.75 C1.27 M0.42

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: As shown in panel B, maximum drawdowns per style are of order 1.8 to 3.1 times the volatility.
claims.claim: All-asset cross-sectional drawdowns are 1.8 to 3.1 times annual volatility; rates momentum is worst at 9.1 times.
claims.reported_result: Table 1B MDD/vol all asset: value -1.8, carry -3.1, mom -2.6; IR momentum -9.1; EQ momentum -4.1

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: The skew is positive for value and momentum and negative for carry.
claims.claim: Cross-sectional carry has negative monthly skew while value and momentum are positive (all asset).
claims.reported_result: Table 1C monthly skew all asset: value 0.09, carry -0.39, mom 0.10; FX carry -1.03

reasoning.question: Should carry, momentum and value be traded directionally (time series) or cross-asset (long-short), and which market conditions decide? It matters because the choice changes net market exposure, which factor risks are hedged and how much of each signal's information is kept.

thesis.statement: Value works best cross-sectionally, momentum best directionally and carry in both; a cross-sectional book is a time-series book with the global factor hedged out, so the right choice depends on whether the global factor trends or mean-reverts and on how correlated signals are relative to assets. All versions combined give high but selection-biased, gross-of-cost Sharpe ratios.

foundations.premise: Forward prices are biased predictors of future spot (Jensen; CAPM forward bias), so a carry premium can exist; with a dividend/value factor the bias is tied to carry.
Carry premia compensate non-diversifiable risks (crash/peso risk in FX, recession and volatility risk) or hedging pressure and inventories in commodities and term premia in rates.
foundations.support: citations (Lustig-Verdelhan, Koijen et al., Keynes, theory of storage)

foundations.premise: Returns persist at 6-12 months and reverse at very short and multi-year horizons; momentum comes from underreaction, flow inertia or disposition effects (or risk exposure).
Asset prices revert toward fundamental anchors (real rate ~ growth, dividend yield ~ ERP, PPP, production cost), slowly, after overshooting.
foundations.support: consumption model, Gordon model, PPP, Dornbusch

foundations.premise: Within an asset class there is a dominant global (market) factor; a market-neutral long-short book hedges it out.
foundations.support: PCA intuition; algebra for linear signals

foundations.premise: Few investors can sit through multi-year underperformance, so simple premia are not arbitraged away.

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: Section 5 claims Sharpe 'close to 2' and eight-fold growth at 15% vol, but the best reported figure is 1.61 (Figure 11 ~7x at unstated vol).
'We tried our hand at six possible explanations' but only five are listed.

Text says 26 equity indices, but the bullet list names 35 (Russell2000, Germany-Tech, Italy, Sweden, Austria, Sensex, Russia, Poland... missing from the start-date table); 'Russia included' in Section 5 yet not in the table.
FX list has 31 entries including USD itself although all are 'versus the USD'; 31 'pairs' vs 30 non-USD currencies.
Commodity carry formula as printed (F_{T1+1y} - F_{T1})/F_{T1+1y} is positive in contango, the opposite sign of the equity and FX carry definitions; probably a typo.

Trade sign for value signals not stated (FX PPP deviation, commodity price ratio); TS 'long if signal positive' undefined for always-positive signals (dividend yield, price ratio around 1) - centring not specified.
FX value averaging window (overline mean) not defined; EWMA crossover applied to price or total return not explicit (C18 implies total return).
All results gross of transaction costs; costs 'discussed later' but never quantified; daily rebalancing with binary signals implies high turnover.
No t-stats or significance tests for Sharpe differences between CS and TS; robustness claims (other configurations, monthly/linear, CPI rates value) given without numbers.
Universe expands over time (many EM series start 1997-2001; S&P value only from 2000), so early-sample results rest on few assets; survivorship admitted.
The 'drivers' (asset vs signal correlation) are proposed but the ex-ante framework is not built or tested; explanation 1 does not explain why value beats momentum cross-sectionally.
Hansen-Heaton-Li dated 1998 in text but 2008 in references; Table 12 IR carry t-stat printed '(10.1)' with negative beta.

reasoning.forward_looking_inputs: (reader) Observable inputs: (1) carry (forward premium, futures slope, swap carry+roll) leads returns over months via risk-premium/forward-bias step; (2) EWMA-crossover trend leads over weeks-months via slow reaction; (3) value anchors (PPP gap, DY, real price vs history, 10Y minus nominal GDP) lead over years via mean reversion. For the CS vs TS choice: the autocorrelation/trend of the asset-class average return and the ratio of average signal correlation to average asset correlation should predict which implementation wins. These stop working if the global factor flips from trending to mean-reverting (hurting TS momentum, helping TS value), if crowding removes the patience premium, or if costs from daily binary rebalancing eat the gross edge.
reader_inferences: (reader) The TS value result likely depends on how the always-positive value signals were centred, which the paper does not state; a demeaned or z-scored version could behave differently.
(reader) The 2015 sample includes a 30-year bond rally and equity bull market, so the TS momentum vs value gap may be regime-specific rather than structural.
(reader) The commodity carry sign as printed would invert the trade; real implementation must have used backwardation-positive carry given the positive commodity carry Sharpe.
(reader) The 'close to 2' Sharpe in Section 5 is probably rhetorical or from an unreported variant; 1.61 is the documented figure.

(reader) Since CS+TS = TS minus half the global mean, a continuous hedge ratio on the global factor (0 to 1) chosen by the global factor's autocorrelation is the natural generalisation the paper points to.
